Formerly, the Emperor’s Mind... [text continues]
The Venerable Master Jizang’s *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā-mukha* takes the *parivṛtti-śāsana* (transformative teaching) as its primary tenet;
while Vinaya Master Chengzhao’s *Jìngxīn-jìguān* (Contemplation of the Precepts for Purifying the Mind) takes the *niyama-śāsana* (prescriptive teaching) as its primary tenet.

As for taking both the transformative and prescriptive teachings as tenets and presenting the aspects of nature (*prakṛti*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in tandem, only National Teacher Xianshou’s *Wàngjìn-huányuán* (Return to the Source upon the Exhaustion of Delusion) encompasses both; thus, it accords with those of the sudden and perfect capacity who [transcend] the provisional and small vehicles.

The flowing [teachings] have been universally bestowed upon my ears. During the Jingyou era, I received this gateway of contemplation at the school of Dharma Master Huipuji (whose name was Qingben) of Kunshan;
both the two scrolls of commentary and one volume of topical outlines were all composed by Dharma-Lamp Master [Zhiyuan].
Nevertheless, regarding the prefaces and various meanings of the contemplations explained therein, although they are entirely excellent, they are not yet exhaustive.

Regarding this excellence, I have summarized the essentials to manage the complexity, selected the words to facilitate practice, and explored the clear and cool purport of the *Śāstra* while seeking out the explanatory terms of the *Vyākhyā*.

By supplementing its deficiencies, I have perfected its merits and achieved a work of comprehensive beauty; therefore, I have titled it the *Sūcāopujie* (Supplementary Explanation of the *Śāstra* and *Vyākhyā*).
As an ancient saying goes: "If one does not cut through a gnarled root, one cannot test the sharpness of a fine tool."
The profound depths of this text cannot be fathomed even by those of versatile talent;
yet, for future descendants to contemplate my ancestral intent, it is here—vivid and clear as the bright sun shining in the sky, never obscured by the darkness of deluded emotions—is this not found?
Written on the third day after the summer retreat in the second year of the Yuanfeng era, the year of Jiwu (1079), at Shanzhu Bao in Yunjian.
Preface to the Commentary.

The single character "cultivation" (xiū) in the title serves as the general thread that unifies the entire work; it refers to the six gates presented in the main text, which together constitute a single contemplation.

Among these, the first three gates (one: essence; two: function; three: pervasiveness) collectively eliminate deluded emotion and reveal understanding, such that a single mote of dust contains and encompasses the void.

The fourth section, which universally distinguishes between empty space and illusory form within the midst [of reality], takes the cultivation of the four kinds of meritorious practices as the preparatory means for permeating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The fifth section enters the five types of *śamatha*, and the sixth section gives rise to the six types of *vipaśyanā*;
only through these does one reach the pinnacle of authentic cultivation. Thus, by entering any single gate, one fully encompasses the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
(The upper part explains the character "cultivation" [xiū]. The nine characters below separately elaborate upon the essential outline; the *Avataṃsaka* is the sūtra that serves as the basis.

"Flower" (*huá*) is a metaphor for the causes of the myriad practices, which adorn the fruit of the ten bodies. "Austere" (*ào*) refers to its vertical depth, acting as the great source for all other scriptures.

"Essential purport" (*zhǐ*) refers to its horizontal breadth, encompassing all other sūtras as its retinue. "The exhaustion of delusion and the return to the source" refers to that which relies [upon the sūtra].

In contemplation, one observes that false phenomena have no inherent substance; this is explained as "exhaustion" (kṣaya), for they ultimately converge back into the One Mind, just as branches return to their source.

Thus, the *Fengshui Fu* (Rhapsody on the Fountainhead) states: "Though ten thousand streams differ, they all emerge from the same source; though the various currents diverge, they all return to the sea.

If one unifies them with the source of the mind, as Qingliang (Xuanzang) said: "If one follows the adventitious dust, one departs and has no place of return; if one perceives the original nature," [one returns].

Thus, one returns to the source and reverts to the root. "The observer's delusions are exhausted and wisdom is extinguished" is a designation for the true nature of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti) being in harmonious integration with all phenomena.
However, this true root cannot be accomplished through effort; it is attained by letting go of effort so that one returns to the root. This profound source cannot be reached through cognition;
it is realized only when cognition is exhausted. Therefore, it is said: "The observer's delusions are exhausted and wisdom is extinguished. Below...
The text also states: "When consciousness is exhausted and views are eliminated, there is coolness; this means that when afflictions are exhausted and principle manifests, all views naturally perish.

Although the wording differs in its brevity and detail, the meaning is identical in its sudden realization. Following the precedent of the title of the *Zhongnan Guan* (Contemplation of Zhongnan), it should have stated:

"Although the wording differs in its brevity and detail, the meaning is identical in its sudden realization across six layers. That this is not explicitly marked here is because the subsequent text comprehensively subsumes them within itself.
This refers to the sixfold gates of contemplation described above; taking one as the primary and the other five as its companions, they are fully detailed in the final chapter.

"Together" (*bing*) means "comprehensive"; "preface" (*xu*) means "to set forth. It sets forth the essential principles of the Dharma and its meaning, as well as the benefits of collecting these contemplations for the sake of sentient beings.
Some say that "Mahāvaipulya" (*Dafangguang*) refers to the Dharma realized, while "Buddhāvataṃsaka" (*Fohuayan*) refers to the person who realizes it.
Now, why does the title here only mark the two characters "capable of realization" (*neng-zheng*)? The answer is:

As for "contemplation," it opens the gate of wisdom for later students and darkly connects them to the ocean of fruition of all Buddhas. Once the gate of wisdom is opened, one spontaneously perceives the infinite, layered interpenetration of the primary and secondary realms;
this is its great function. As for clarifying that within this single sūtra and three great divisions, all are *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Vaipulya),...

The *Zhoubian* (Commentary on the Title) explains the seven characters of the sutra’s title by simultaneously indicating cause and effect, Buddha and the *Avataṃsaka*, person and dharma, and by presenting both the metaphor and the reality;
it encompasses both essence and function, as well as cause and fruit, such that its principles are exhaustive and its meanings perfect.

Now, this present work adopts a more concise title, taking only the two characters "Huayan" (*Avataṃsaka*) as the basis for the sutra upon which it relies. If this is the case, then regarding the *Fajie Guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm):
Why are exactly six characters used for the title? Now, the broad and the concise follow different paths, and the methods of composition vary;

since the structural forms are manifold, they cannot be standardized by a single rule. If one criticizes Xianshou for omitting the four characters "Dafangguangfo" (Mahāvaipulya-buddha) from his title, why not criticize Dixin for omitting the two characters "bingxu" (together with the preface) beneath his title?
Former scholars have remarked that such omissions are difficult to reconcile, subtly disparaging them as being forced or artificial.
"To excavate this is also my ambition.

"Jing" refers to Chang'an; Zhang Yan’s commentary on the *Hanshu* states that a place where the terrain is exceptionally high is called a "jing. The *Zuo Zhuan* says, "None can rival it in greatness," where "jing" signifies "greatness.
Prior to the eras of Tang and Yu, the residences of emperors and kings were frequently referred to as being "in the capital" (*du*) of such-and-such a place.
The records state that Fuxi and Shennong both had their capitals in Chen; this is that very place.

As for "Dajianfu" (Great Jianfu), there were many monasteries in the Tang dynasty known as Jianfu, some of which were simply called "Jianfu," so the word "Da" (Great) was used here to distinguish it. "Jian" (荐) means to offer; it signifies performing rites to bring merit to one's deceased parents.
This temple was built by Emperor Zhongzong of the Tang dynasty. According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*, Zhongzong...
With a heart of boundless longing, he sought to cultivate the causes for merit; thus, he first established Jianfu Monastery in Chang’an.

As the construction did not proceed as desired and the laborers were burdened by toil, he issued an edict appointing Zhang Xi, Minister of Works, together with the Vinaya Master Shi Dao’an to oversee the project.
They extensively opened up expedient means and widely practiced compassion; people came to serve like children, their labors free from lingering burdens, and expenses were kept modest.
Emperor Gaozong greatly praised his meritorious service. "Sì" (temple) is a Sanskrit term, *vihāra*, which here means "place of dwelling";

it is where those who have left the household life travel and reside. The *Guǎngyá* states that a sì is a place of administration. The *Shìmíng* says that within it, those who manage affairs continue their work.
"Śramaṇa" is translated as "stopping evil," meaning there is no evil that is not stopped; this is the general designation for the sons of Śākya.
Furthermore, the next two characters are his posthumous name (ming-hui). According to the epitaph composed by Yan Chaoyin, Vice Director of the Secretariat, it states:
"The National Teacher’s surname was Kang; his name was Fazang. For generations they had inherited the position of Chancellor of the Kingdom of Kangju.

His grandfather came from Kangju to court; his father was posthumously titled Duke of the Left Attendant by the Imperial Court. When the National Teacher was only sixteen years old, he refined one of his fingers..."
After King Aśoka’s relics had been offered as objects of veneration, he then traveled to Dabaiya, where he deeply contemplated the profound mystery.
Hearing that Master Yan of Yunhua Temple was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he threw himself at his feet as a superior disciple.

He took up the practice of receiving water in a flask and the causal conditions of casting a mustard seed through a needle’s eye; thus his fame spread throughout the world and his reputation reached the imperial court, attracting the patronage of the Princess of Rong.

When the Empress Dowager suddenly passed away and the period of mourning for hempen sackcloth had not yet ended, the Empress Dowager Shengtian extensively propagated the Buddha-vehicle and widely opened the treasury of the Dharma.
The National Teacher, having registered his name within the palace precincts and shaved his head at the Daochang Monastery, resided at Taiyuan Temple.
During the Zhengsheng era, by imperial decree, he collaborated with the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda to translate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra until the Shenlong era.
Among the Dragon Kings, he likewise translated the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*. It is the sole refuge for the Sages and the sole object of dedication for the Sovereign.
Thereupon, an imperial decree was issued appointing him as the Preceptor of Bodhisattva Precepts.

His Majesty the Retired Emperor, having cast off the myriad affairs of state and lifted his robes from the four seas, also received the precepts and lectured on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* more than thirty times, as well as the *Brahmajāla*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Ghanavyūha*, and *Udānavarga* sūtras.
The Master Xìn possessed commentaries on the scriptures that were transmitted throughout the four quarters.
On the fourteenth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Xiāntián era (the *rénzǐ* year), he passed away at Dà Jiànfú Temple in the Western Capital at the age of seventy.

On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of that same year, he was buried at Shénhuó Yuán, south of Huáyán Temple. The Emperor’s grief was as if struck by lightning, and his sorrow was as if he had lost something precious; thus, he issued this edict.

It was said: "The State Preceptor’s virtue and deeds, his natural endowment of luminous clarity, his realization of the principles, his eloquence, his hidden wisdom, and his awakened, harmonious mind have extensively opened the gate of the raft of parables and fully expounded the teachings of the transmitted lamp.
He manifested responses according to conditions, and his transformative influence has now reached its end.

Although he is comparable to a true master who has entered quiescence and realized the emptiness of non-arising, it is appropriate that the imperial court provide a decree to honor this worthy man as he concludes his life."

He was posthumously bestowed the title of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing) and granted one thousand two hundred bolts of silk for his funeral expenses, with the rites conducted according to the monastic precedent;

all other matters were provided by the state. As for the fact that he presided over the assembly and adjudicated the teachings, uniquely attaining their profound mysteries, his systematization was comprehensive and his exegesis of the scriptures illuminated both past and present, as fully detailed in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Sacred Song* (*Sengzhuan*) and the *Biographies of the Seven Patriarchs*.
The author’s clarity is evident; the *Record of Music* (*Yueji*) states: "The creator is called a sage."
The commentator says: "Although it is clear that under the name and taboo characters of the Emperor, the term 'compiled' (ji) is used; why then does the current text say 'commentary' (shu)?

This means that because the preface was not fully manifest, there is no doubt that the initial compilation followed established precedents; for this reason, the term 'compiled' is not used here. The "Fulいた教" (Mǎnjiào) refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.
The passage originates from the Northern Edition of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; that sūtra clarifies that the "half-syllables" (bàn zì) refer to the Hīnayāna.
Because "riding upon the full syllable" refers to the Mahāyāna, Qingliang (Chengguan) stated: "The 'half' and 'full' are metaphors; the 'great' and 'small' are the dharmas.
As for the term "inconceivable," this teaching does not take the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as its primary tenet, and thus it cannot be grasped by the ordinary mind.

Regarding the word "to look" (*kui*), the *Zuozhuan* says: "To lift one's feet and gaze. A single mote of dust manifests instantaneously, as the *Pranidhānapatala* (Chapter on Vows) states: "Within a single mote of dust..."
In each of the assemblies of bodhisattvas throughout the various lands, these words are also found throughout the great scriptures.

In the subsequent section, the National Preceptor cites the *Sūtra on the Manifestation of Buddha-Bodies in All Lands*, which says: "Into every single atom within all the atoms of the Flower Treasury World, Buddhas enter;

for the sake of all sentient beings, they universally manifest spiritual transformations, such is the Dharma of Vairocana. This is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), as explained in the *Awakening of Faith*.
The Commentary clarifies that there are five schools within the systems of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: (1) the School of Phenomenal Adherence to Characteristics;

(2) the School of True Emptiness and Signlessness; (3) the School of Yogācāra Dharmalakṣaṇa; (4) the School of Tathāgatagarbha Dependent Origination; and (5) the School of Perfect Fusion and Endowed Virtue. Thus, Xianshou said:
"The Perfect Master possesses both principal and attendant aspects, complete and infinitely layered; this is precisely the Great Sūtra. And he further stated:
"Inconceivable" (*aprameya*) means that this teaching cannot be fathomed by words, as it transcends names and phrases. "Contemplation" (*guan*) means to observe.

"The subtlest hairs are all manifested together" refers to even the smallest single hair; the *Xiànxiàng pǐn* (Chapter on Manifesting Signs) states: "Within a single pore of the Tathāgata, there are all the Buddhas sitting beneath their trees amidst the dust-motes of all lands.
This is cited from the *Shēn xiàn chàtǔ jīng* (Sūtra on the Body Manifesting Buddha-lands), which says: "A single hair..."
Within a single pore there are immeasurable lands, each with its four continents, four great oceans, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains;

it is likewise so for all [lands], which appear therein without crowding or overflowing. The preceding phrase indicates a single mote of dust in terms of the external *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (retributive environment);

the following phrase reveals even a tiny hair in terms of the internal *vipāka-phala* (retributive body). That they are manifested simultaneously is a sudden appearance; the phrasing of the text is merely slightly altered. Thus, the *Yìhǎi* (Ocean of Meaning) says:

The one and the many completely encompass one another; by observing a single speck of dust, all things are suddenly revealed. When looking at a mere hair, everything appears simultaneously. Someone asked:
"What is the difference between the teachings of the *Pūrṇa* (the full/complete) and the essence of the *Vṛtta* (the perfect/circular) school? The answer, as stated in the *Great Commentary*, is:

"In establishing the teachings (*śāsana*), one must necessarily distinguish between the stages of severance and realization. In establishing the school (*siddhānta*), one merely clarifies the differences in what is being honored; therefore, there is a distinction."

"Er" (then/however) is a term of indefiniteness used to apply [the principle] according to the division of essence; it is the contemplation that brings one to rest. It is not a lack of differentiation, for it refers to the contemplative illumination of both nature and characteristics.
Thus, the *Yihai* (Ocean of Meaning) says: "The chapters on the marks of essence and the opening of function are the categories that assist the Path."

For the most part, it clarifies that the power of the distinctions among conditions arises from their nature; that phenomena manifest based on principle is the very cessation (*śamatha*) of contemplation.

To possess the form of a single limit means to bring all conditions to rest. The *Yìhǎi* (Ocean of Meaning) further states: "Dharmas have no boundaries; when they manifest, they must do so simultaneously.

Principle does not obstruct differentiation, for manifestation and concealment share a single limit. Alternatively, it is said that function is divided according to substance, which refers to what follows below.
Regarding the statement that "the essence is one and its functions are two," since the essence and function have already been introduced, why not describe the three pervasions and four virtues?
This is because such a correspondence would be overly contrived;

therefore, they are not adopted here. It is like the six phrases in the passage below: the first two phrases present both the dharma and the metaphor simultaneously, while the next two phrases explain the metaphor. Subsequently...
The second section explains the Dharma. Regarding the first point, "the arising of illness prompts the emergence of medicine, and the production of delusion leads to the establishment of wisdom":

this means that when illness breaks out, medicine must be used to treat it; when delusion arises, wisdom must be established to dispel it. According to the *Wuxiang ji* (Collection on Signlessness), there are two kinds of illness:
first, discursive thought (*ālambana-cintā*); second, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Discursive thought refers to the two types of mental states, good and evil, though they differ from one another.

Since liberation is neither [of these two], they are collectively categorized as "indeterminate objects of cognition. Although they do not take good, evil, or other such phenomena as their objects, they are nonetheless not the true mind;
both are merely states of dull stagnation. (If other schools maintain that the indeterminate is the true mind, how does this differ from mistaking rubble for genuine gold?

There are also two types of this state: first, profound stillness (*jijie*); second, alert clarity (*xingxing*). Profound stillness refers to the non-recollection of external objects, whether good or evil.

"Vigilance" (xingxing) refers to not giving rise to states such as dullness, fixation, or neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, one uses "stillness" (jiji) to counteract discursive thought and "vigilance" to counteract dullness and fixation;
these two practices of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together counteract them. This is precisely what was previously referred to as the "establishment of wisdom from deluded arising.

Thus, "deluded arising" refers to the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), while the "establishment of wisdom" refers to the two wisdoms of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and suchness-in-extent (*yāvadbhāva-jñāna*).

When analytical wisdom (*prajñā*) destroys afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no objective referent; when wisdom as-it-is (*yathāvadbhāva-jñāna*) destroys the knowable (*jñeya*), there is no dull stagnation.

Thus, the reason for citing the two diseases and two medicines from the *Nirnimitta* [chapter] to clarify the text is that it accords with the doctrine of the two wisdoms and two obscurations held by various schools.
The two lines beginning with "the forgetting of the disease" and "the forgetting of the medicine" explain the analogy; that is to say, once the two diseases of dullness and distraction have been...

When [the medicine] is forgotten, both the medicines of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are likewise forgotten; thus, the "empty fist" is used as a metaphor for forgetting the medicine.
The "stopping of the crying" is a metaphor for forgetting the illness. Qianfu said: "It is like grasping an empty fist to deceive and entice a child.
Once the child’s wailing has ceased, one opens the fist and extends the hand—could there be any object there? "Child" (*rou*) refers to an infant; "gua-gua" is the sound of their crying.

"Solitary weeping" refers to the sound [of grief]. "The mind penetrates and phenomena penetrate"—the following two phrases explain "phenomena. This means that when the mind penetrates, the two types of wisdom both vanish;

when phenomena penetrate, the two obstacles are simultaneously extinguished. Since the obstacle of wisdom is stilled and subject and object merge into one, the text cites empty space as a metaphor for the pervasiveness of nature (*dharmatā*).
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For example, empty space is universally pervasive throughout all things," and it further says: "Phenomena..."
The nature pervades all places.

"Already awakened and already enlightened" means that once the delusions of dullness and distraction have been suddenly eliminated through awakening, the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is likewise realized as being equally extinguished;
thus, what is there to be obstructed and what is there to be penetrated? Regarding the "hundred negations," Master Sengzhao says:
There is but one principle which is termed "non-dharma" (adharma), yet because it does not stop at a single [negation], it is called the "hundred negations" (*śata-apavāda*).

As for "clinging to objects" (*ālambana*), it refers to the subtle movement of deluded appearances as they cling to all phenomena. Furthermore, the *Bishuo ji* states that these "hundred negations" are elucidated in terms of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of existence and non-existence, identity and difference—namely:
existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence. Each of these is further negated, resulting in the hundred negations.
The "not existent" [category] constitutes one set of four propositions; when this is applied equally to the other cases, they collectively form sixteen.

Furthermore, for each of the past, present, and future, there are sixteen, totaling forty-eight. When the forty-eight for those already arisen and those not yet arisen are combined with the four fundamental [propositions], they total one hundred non-existences.
However, according to the introductory text which excludes such additions and subtractions, the four propositions are clarified by means of the four types of denial (*apavāda*).

First, the adherence to existence is the slander of superimposition; second, the adherence to non-existence is the slander of denial; third, the adherence to both existence and non-existence is the slander of contradiction;
and fourth, the adherence to neither existence nor non-existence is the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Here, "increase and decrease" refers to two of these four types of slander.

Now, because the mind has attained penetration and phenomena have attained penetration, all discursive thought is severed and words forgotten; thus, the hundredfold errors of the branches and leaves are all extinguished by means of the four fundamental [slanders].
Sentences are suddenly extinguished.
Therefore, regarding the term "attains" (*de*): "thereby" (*xià gù*) refers to the reason; "attains" (*dé*) means to acquire it for oneself.

Because one's prior nature, mind, and the penetration of phenomena have already been awakened and realized, one thereby acquires [the state where] medicine and disease vanish and stillness and agitation merge.

This passage uses stillness and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as a metaphor for medicine, and movement and distraction as a metaphor for illness. This is a case of interpreting distinct phrases separately and then returning them to a unified whole:

when both the medicine and the illness are simultaneously extinguished, one realizes entry into the profound principle (*mūla-tattva*); when the nature of stillness and the appearance of distraction are both fused, one returns to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

"Privately observed" (*qie jian*) means that I have privately observed the teachings and meanings of the Great Sūtra. "The profound framework is vast and expansive" (*xuan gang hao huan*) refers to the teaching as the expressive medium (*neng quan*);
"vast and expansive" (*hao huan*) describes the appearance of water spreading widely, hence the *Great Commentary* (*Da shu*) says, "the waves and ripples of the ocean of teaching.

"The wondrous purport is subtle and elusive" (*xi wei*) refers to the meaning expressed (*suo quan*); "subtle and elusive" (*xi wei*) is synonymous with "rarefied and silent" (*xi yi*), as the *Prajñā Treatise* says, "in accord with... [and so forth].

How could one exhaust the source of the realm of the Ineffable and the Unmanifest? How could one possibly fathom the limits of that which is expressed by the Explanatory? "Source" refers to the initial emergence of water;
"limits" refers to the extremity where something is rarely exhausted. "Rarely" means few or scanty. "Extremity" refers to the ultimate point.

Because true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the wisdom that performs the contemplation, it resides within the mind; because the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the object of contemplation, it dwells before one’s eyes.

Furthermore, since true emptiness is without thought yet thoughts constantly arise as objects of cognition, and the limit of reality is formless yet forms arise and are inverted into names and marks, the *Pao-tsang lun* states:
"True wisdom is hidden within the sphere of cognitive objects, while the Dharma-body..."
"Hidden within the form-egg" (*rūpa-aṇḍa*) refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is another name for the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

"Comprehensively encompassing" (*tǒngshōu*) means to gather and include all. "Profound and mysterious" (*xuánnà*) refers to the aforementioned vast and deep fundamental principle (*xuángāng*). "Encompassing and binding" (*bāokuò*) is synonymous with "including and tying together.
"The Great Source" (*dàzōng*) refers to the aforementioned wondrous intent that is subtle and elusive. "Bringing forth the great scripture from amidst the dust" refers to the Great Sutra.

The Parable of Dust Containing Sutra Scrolls (The text consists of two sections; the first is the Dharma-exposition). The Sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere. Why is this?
There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata. (The Commentary states: This is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature pervading all equally.

The reason we know that Buddha-wisdom is omnipresent is that there is not a single sentient being who lacks original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), for their essence is no different from that of all Buddhas. It is only because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments [that they do not realize it].

Yet they do not realize it (because they are inverted and thus not clear; how could one say it does not exist? It is like a strong man who, being deluded, loses his forehead jewel—does this mean the treasure was not within his skin?). If one is free from false imagination (*vikalpa*), then all-knowledge (*sarvajñāna*), spontaneous knowledge (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and unimpeded knowledge (*asaṅga-jñāna*) will manifest before one.

(This means: if there were first no freedom from inversion, how could there be [realization]? Since one is now free from inversion, the clarity is revealed as having been inherently present and never non-existent. It is like a poor man finding a jewel—it was not bestowed upon him only now. "Spontaneous knowledge" is the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-ārya-jñāna*).

"Unimpeded knowledge" is the state where beginning and end are non-dual, transcending the two obstacles. Two parables: O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: *Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary analogy regarding the loss of a forehead jewel by a strong man due to delusion, followed by an analogy regarding a poor man finding a jewel. These illustrate that the inherent wisdom is not newly created but revealed through the removal of delusion.*
Suppose there were a great sutra scroll (a metaphor for the boundless Buddha-wisdom and the perfection of innate virtues), equal in size to a trichiliocosm,

upon which all the events of the great thousandfold world system were inscribed in their entirety, even down to the point where the dimensions of the writing were exactly equal [to the objects they described] (inscribing each thing according to its specific object means that wisdom accords with reality).
Although this great sutra scroll is as vast as a great thousandfold world system, it remains entirely contained within a single minute atom.
Regarding "within a mote of dust" (the phrase "a hidden mote of dust" has three meanings in brief: first, because delusion obscures the truth; second, because the small contains the great;

third, because the one possesses the many), it is as with one minute mote of dust, so it is with all minute motes of dust (all motes of dust means that there is not a single sentient being who does not possess Buddha-wisdom).

At that time, there was a person whose wisdom was clear and penetrating, who had fully accomplished the pure divine eye, and who saw this sutra scroll within the minute mote of dust through diligent effort.
With power, one shatters those atoms to bring forth this sutra scroll, thereby enabling them to obtain great benefit. (3) The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise thus:
immeasurable, unimpeded, and universally able to benefit all sentient beings. (Combined with the above: "The many matters of copying") It is fully present within the bodies of sentient beings;
yet, because of the delusive thoughts and attachments of ordinary fools, they neither know nor perceive it. (Sentient beings' bodies and delusive thoughts)
[Combined with the preceding "dust"] At that time, the Tathāgata, with the unobstructed eye of pure wisdom, universally surveyed all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm and spoke these words:
"How marvelous! How marvelous! These sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet due to ignorance and delusion, they neither know nor see it.
I shall instruct them in the Noble Path," and so forth. [Combined with the preceding "the Tathāgata's single eye of wisdom"].

The celestial eye is that which benefits sentient beings through all the sūtras. Regarding the detailed citations from the sūtras and commentaries provided above with individual annotations, this is because both the prefaces to the *Extensive* and *Abridged* Commentaries on the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, as well as the two sections of the *Chanquan Guanyuan Men* (The Gate of Explaining Chan through Contemplation), briefly cite the sūtras and have them explained by Guifeng;

these sometimes differ from the original commentary by Qingliang. Furthermore, since the subsequent section where Xianshou again cites the verses to explain their meaning is also brief, [the citations here are likewise concise].
Now, this commentary on the sutra records these matters in full, hoping that future generations will examine them in detail.
Regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma within a single pore, a verse from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Within a single pore, there are inconceivable lands as numerous as atoms;
each of these various abodes contains a Universal Illuminator (Samantaprabha) amidst an assembly, expounding the wondrous Dharma. Furthermore, it is like Sudhana’s final quest for a spiritual friend.
When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra minutely observed the body of Samantabhadra,
he saw within a single pore unspeakably unspeakable oceans of Buddha-fields, even as many as the atoms within the Buddha-fields seen by Sudhana,
where he visited and attended upon countless spiritual friends to accumulate wisdom; yet compared to this, what Samantabhadra attained in that brief vision was a hundredfold.
It does not equal even a fraction of one, nor even a *niṣadha* fraction; from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until that of Samantabhadra,

the succession of oceans of lands entered by Sudhana in the interim is surpassed now by what is entered in a single instant within a single pore of Samantabhadra by an unspeakably unspeakable multiple, and this continues until the very end.
Even throughout the limits of the future, one cannot know the various oceans of lands, oceans of Buddhas, and oceans of assemblies of Bodhisattvas within a single pore;
since these are called "oceans of Buddhas" and "oceans of assemblies," is it not the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurring within that hair-pore?
The enlightened one’s virtue flourishes on that very day, demonstrating his sudden capacity (*tongji*). The *Commentary on the Vows and Practices* (*Xingyuan shu*) states:
"If one enters its gate, one is equal to all Buddhas in a single morning. The *Chapter on Pure Conduct* (*Fanxing pin*) states:

"If Bodhisattvas can accord with such a gate of contemplation, they will not give rise to even a single conceptual understanding regarding all phenomena, and all Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before them at the first inception [of the path]."
At the very moment of thought, one attains perfect enlightenment and achieves the body of wisdom, not through awakening by means of another;

this too is the absence of mind, where the essence reaches its ultimate limit in a single thought-moment, and one immediately accords with the Buddha-family. For the deluded, hope is cut off after many lifetimes; thus, the *Commentary on the Root Verses of Practice and Vows* (*Xingyuan shu*) states:
"If one loses the essential meaning, one merely cultivates causes throughout vast eons. The *Chapter on Manifestation* (*Chuxian pin*) says: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva..."

Even if one practices the six *pāramitās* for hundreds of thousands of billions of *kalpas*, if one does not hear this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty and power, or if having heard it at some time, one does not believe, does not understand, does not comply with, and does not enter into it, one cannot be called a true Bodhisattva;
such a person is merely practicing through effort, and though many kalpas may pass, their practice will ultimately end in failure and ruin. This is the realization of the essential meaning.

"Mountains and peaks are easily moved" is a metaphor for the previous sudden faculty (*tongji*), where formlessness is called "wondrous awakening. "The main thoroughfare is not blocked by mountains and rivers":

here, "mountain" refers to a peak, such as Mount Tai, which is the Eastern Peak (*Dongyue*). "Deviation from the fundamental principle makes even a *zi* or a *zhu* difficult to enter" is a metaphor for the previous gradual root (*jian-gen*), where formlessness is further described:
"to be deluded by names and stuck in forms creates a separation of even a thread or a hair. Eight *zhu* make one *zi*, and twenty-four *zhu* make one *zi*.

"Of two" means a pair. "Zhuo" (輾) means exclusive or single-minded. "Xuanpi" (旋披) refers to searching through thoroughly. "Wanggao" (往誥) refers to the scriptural proclamations translated during the Jin dynasty;

"gao" (誥) means to announce or inform, that is, to instruct so as to bring about understanding. "Dian" (覿) means to observe from a distance. "Jiuzhang" (舊章) refers to the ancient commentaries and exegeses. "Zhang" (章) refers to the chapters.

That which fully encompasses the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka refers to the three collections of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, which correspond to the three trainings of precepts (śīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).
In the fourth section below, the four kinds of conduct and virtue clarify the training in precepts;

in the fifth section, entering the five forms of tranquility (śamatha) clarifies the training in concentration; and in the sixth section, giving rise to the six forms of insight (vipaśyanā) clarifies...

This gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is indeed the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). It encompasses both the trainings in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet it is specifically categorized as the training in wisdom.

Regarding this specific categorization as the training in wisdom, there are two explanations: first, according to the main text, the six gates are presented individually, yet they collectively constitute a single contemplation;

second, according to the supplementary records, when one arouses the mind and practices, it is called "contemplation," whereas when practice is spontaneously established, it is called "wisdom. Therefore, it is designated as the training in wisdom.

"Simultaneously encompassing both precepts (śīla) and meditative concentration (samādhi)" means that one first employs the four types of virtuous practices as skillful means, and subsequently cultivates the five forms of stillness (śamatha);

thus, precepts and concentration are "encompassed together. Furthermore, if the original text frequently translates [terms] through question-and-answer formats and repeatedly cites the *Aśrayaparivṛtti-śāstra* (*Qixin lun*) as proof, then it properly belongs to the Śāstra Piṭaka.
If one understands this distinction between the "encompassed" and the "primary," the other two Piṭakas—the Sūtra and Vinaya—can be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, one should know that the Three Piṭakas are categorized according to the Dharma, while the Two Piṭakas are categorized according to persons. Now, observing the text here, it pertains primarily to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, while also encompassing the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
This is because the subsequent text explains how the transformative teaching universally causes sentient beings to undergo suffering on their behalf, which belongs to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka;
and it explains that the five aggregates have no master, clarifying the emptiness of persons, which belongs to the Śrāvaka Piṭaka. Thus it is established.
Within the teachings, both the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Four-Part Vinaya* cite the Bodhisattva-piṭaka as the primary [collection] and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka as secondary.
If one were to follow the precedent of the text from Zhongnan Mountain’s contemplation practice (*guanwen*), it would differ greatly from this:

that contemplation is based on persons, and since it is specifically for Bodhisattvas, there is no Śrāvaka-piṭaka; yet when based on the Dharma, it includes both the Sūtra and Śāstra piṭakas, though lacking the Vinaya-piṭaka. Why is this? It clarifies three...

In the Gate of Profound Contemplation (*gūjìng guānmén*), the study of wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) is primary while the study of concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is secondary; because the four types of conduct and virtue are not expounded therein, there is no study of ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).

Regarding those who rely on the sublime purport of the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*): "vehicle" (*yāna*) takes "transporting" as its meaning. These five powers have varying magnitudes, and their transportations have varying distances and proximities.
The first is the Vehicle of Humans (*pudgala-yāna*), which refers to the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; it transports sentient beings across [the sea of suffering].

Regarding the three miserable realms, the human path, and the two heavens, the Vehicle of the Ten Wholesome Actions and the Four Dhyānas and Eight Samādhis is called the "Superior Vehicle," for it carries sentient beings across the four continents and reaches the higher realms.
The Vehicle of the Three Śrāvakas refers to the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths;
the Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas refers to the Dharma-gate of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; both carry sentient beings across the three [miserable realms].
From the realms leading to *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa, through the attainment of the state of an Arhat and Pratyekabuddha,

up to the five vehicles of the Bodhisattvas— namely, the Dharma-gate of compassion, wisdom, and the six *pāramitās* which transport sentient beings across the three realms and the spheres of the three vehicles to the further shore of unsurpassed bodhi and Great Parinirvāṇa—
if one examines the meaning of these five vehicles within the Middle Way, it is extremely profound and hidden. Now...

These two meanings may be reconciled in two ways: first, by relying on the extant text, which mutually subsumes them; second, by following the Great Commentary (*Dàshù*), which assigns them to the vehicles (*yāna*).
However, observing the extant text, it clarifies that the three refuges and five precepts are the bridge for crossing the sea of suffering and the foundation for proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*.
"Crossing the sea of suffering" subsumes the preceding two, namely the human vehicle (*manuṣya-yāna*) and the celestial vehicle (*deva-yāna*); "proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*" subsumes the latter.
The three refer to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; therefore, one first relies on the extant text to mutually encompass and harmonize them.
According to the *Qingliang Shidi Shu* (Commentary on the Ten Stages by Qingliang), they are: first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); second, the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*);

third, the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). These three are correlated with the mundane vehicles of humans and devas. Fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*); fifth, the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*); sixth, the Stage of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*); seventh...

The Stage of Far-Reaching Travel (Dūramgamā-bhūmi): these four are based upon the three vehicles of the supramundane; therefore, they are subsequently subsumed under the "vehicles" according to the Great Commentary (*Mahā-ṭīkā*).
Regarding the phrase "verbose expressions must be excised": "excise" (*xiāo*) refers to deletion, while "add" (*bǐ*) refers to augmentation.
What is now termed "verbose expressions must be excised" means precisely deletion. [Where there are] omissions in meaning, they are... [restored].
This is what is meant by "addition" (*āropa*).

Although the initial compilation was undoubtedly a matter of free interpretation (*yoga*), how much more so is it the case that the original regulations have a basis, which constitutes a "subtraction" (*apavāda*)?
"Initial compilation" refers to the first gathering; as in the *Dìxīn Guānjí Yì*, where the meaning is gathered but the text is not. "Undoubtedly" refers to within the text.

The Master said: "When one has exhausted principle and fully realized nature, what doubt can there be? Now, I have gathered the words of the former sages as rules and standards to serve as my reliance;
thus, I eliminate all redundant and divergent expressions. The *Zhouyi* says: 'He whose mind is doubtful has divergent expressions.

Here, 'exhausting this sea of nature' refers to the awakened nature being like an ocean, spoken of in terms of its depth and vastness. 'Sublime practices are like a forest' speaks of their towering height. [End of] Section Three.
Without further elaboration, I shall now separately explain the six gates above. First, "the limit is brilliantly clear" explains what was previously stated as being a single contemplation;

that is, the Single True Limit (ekabhūtakoṭi) is brilliantly clear and manifest. Some say this refers collectively to a single contemplation, generally termed "returning to the source," which also possesses its own logic.
"Hope to return from the lost path" means that just as a person who has lost their way and headed west toward the east hopes for a return home.

"Sentiment is like the morning sun": "sentiment" refers to the Dharma of emotion, while "sun" is a metaphor. For when one contemplates the mind and achieves illumination, emotional calculations are entirely dispelled;

this is just as when the morning sun rises in brilliance, the darkening mist is instantly cleared away. "Wearing the Way" is equivalent to "bearing the Way. "Wearing" refers to the jade belt, which is a matter of ritual propriety (*li*).

It is said: "In all cases where one wears a girdle, there must be a pendant. The Way is the root of one's nature and virtue; it must not be separated from one for even a moment—what else could these pendants be?
Regarding the "gentleman," Confucius said to Duke Ai of Lu: "One's words must be loyal and trustworthy, yet the heart must not be frivolous;

benevolence and righteousness must reside within the person, yet the countenance must not be boastful; thought and deliberation must be penetrating and clear, yet the speech must not be dogmatic; one must practice with sincerity and hold fast to the Way."
Yet to be self-strengthening and never-ceasing—this is the scholar-monk (*junzi ru*). Now, it is likewise so: what is called "name" must correspond to "reality," and the mind must not be frivolous;
the precepts and dharma reside within one's person, yet one does not boast of their appearance; concentration and wisdom further augment one another, yet one’s speech is not monopolistic;

one transmits the bequeathed teachings while being self-strengthening and never-ceasing—this is the noble monk (*junzi seng*). Only those who look down and examine these matters minutely [will understand].

The scholar-monk Sengfu followed his heart toward the Way and practiced it extensively; "extensively" (*guǎng*) refers to its detailed nature, while "焉" (*yān*) is a particle used to mark the end of a clause.

Although the names were listed at the outset, these six gates arise in a specific sequence: since there is nothing that precedes the fundamental essence (*běntǐ*) regarding the arising of Buddhas or the delusion and awakening of sentient beings, [the essence is treated first].
First, it is bestowed to manifest the essence; since the development of the essential nature depends upon wondrous function, second, it is bestowed to give rise to that function.
Because wondrous function universally pervades every dust-mote, third, it is bestowed to demonstrate its omnipresence.
Because one practices karmic deeds based on the environment that is thus omnipresent, fourth, it is bestowed to cultivate virtuous conduct. This refers to the cultivation of virtuous conduct.

Because one personally abides in the cessation that harmonizes the mind, the fifth stage bestows upon them Great Cessation (*mahāśamatha*). Although the gate of cessation is quiescent, the observing mind is constantly luminous;
therefore, the sixth stage bestows upon them Wondrous Observation (*vipaśyanā*). The first reveals the essential nature of the single essence;

its great purport is precisely the *Avataṃsaka*’s True Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of One Reality. The second gives rise to two functions: first, the function of the eternally abiding Ocean Seal, which clarifies the self-...

Furthermore, regarding the arising of two functions from this [essence], first is the "Ocean Seal of Forest-like Constancy" function;
citing two verses from the Sūtra, this also subsumes the first "Perfectly Radiant Ocean Seal Samādhi Gate. Second is the "Dharmadhātu Perfection... [and so forth].

This is according to the classification of the scripture by Qingliang. Furthermore, within these aforementioned four verses, three gates are subsumed:
first, they subsume the fourth gate, the *Vipula-pūjā-niḥsaraṇa-samādhi*, because the verse directly cited states: "Adorning and purifying inconceivable lands, making offerings... [and so forth].
